summary: Registers the media types application/gzip and application/zlib for data compressed with the gzip and zlib formats. This lets protocols and software label such content properly. It is informational and not an Internet Standards Track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC registers standard labels for gzip and zlib compressed data. The labels help software identify which compressed format a data stream uses.

questions: what is the application/gzip media type
what media types identify gzip and zlib
what are the first bytes of gzip data
subtitle: Registers application/gzip and application/zlib for compressed data.

tldr.problem: Applications used several informal media type names for gzip-compressed data, and there was no registration for zlib data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers application/gzip for gzip streams and application/zlib for zlib streams; both use DEFLATE.
tldr.outcome: The IANA Application Media Types registry includes both media types.

today: RFC 6713 is an Informational registration of application/zlib and application/gzip. The unit metadata lists no update or replacement.

sections.title: Why Register Compression Media Types
sections.content:
zlib and gzip are widely used compression formats, both based on DEFLATE. The RFC says zlib is a stream format, while gzip adds header and trailer fields suited to a file format.

Applications had used several informal names for gzip data. This memo defines application/gzip and application/zlib as the media types for the respective formats.
sections.plainLanguage: zlib and gzip both compress data, but use different formats. This memo gives each format a registered media type name.

sections.title: The application/zlib and application/gzip Types
sections.content:
The application/zlib media type describes a block of data compressed using the zlib format. The registration lists binary encoding and describes the first byte as usually 0x78, with other listed possibilities.

The application/gzip media type describes data compressed using gzip. Its registration lists the first two bytes as 0x1f and 0x8b and the file extension as gz.
sections.plainLanguage: Use application/zlib for zlib data and application/gzip for gzip data. The RFC also lists byte patterns that can help identify each format.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that compressed data may contain arbitrary binary data, including hostile executable code. Data claiming to use gzip or zlib may not actually follow those formats, and fields such as lengths or pointers may contain arbitrary values.

Applications should treat incoming data skeptically and consult the security sections of the underlying format specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: A file that claims to be compressed data may be malformed or harmful. Applications should check it carefully before using it.
